To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
age-related deficits in task-switching performance may not be evident when memory load is low, stimulus-response mappings are highly practiced, and task sets are not highly complex.
age-related deficits were not found in task-switching processes when the task involved well-learned stimulus-response mappings and low memory load.
the age-related differences in switch costs for the prosaccade and the antisaccade tasks are not significant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of the ability to inhibit responses.
the effects of aging on cognitive processes involved in the control and execution of goal directed behavior.
the study of age differences in task-switching performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
age-related deficits in task-switching performance are not found in all situations.
there are no age-related differences in task-switching performance when stimulus-response mapping is well learned and the memory load is low.
there is no age-related decline in task-switching processes, but rather a decline in the ability to maintain more than one task in working memory.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

age-related deficits in task-switching processes are found in situations in which task-switching demands are high (e.g., when memory load is high or stimulus-response mappings are arbitrary), and age-related sparing is observed in situations in which the task-switching demands is low (e.g., memory load is low or stimulus-response mappings have been well learned).
age-related deficits in task-switching performance are found when memory load is high and/or when stimulus-response mappings are arbitrary.
the switch costs for both prosaccade and anti-saccade tasks are not affected by aging.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the age-related differences in task-switching performance are dependent on the task used.
the switch cost in antisaccade task is age invariant.
task-switching processes can be preserved in old age, even in situations in which the cognitive load of the tasks is high.
